stem: A 35-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents with depression (PHQ-9 16) that has not responded to quetiapine 300mg nocte for 8 weeks. She refuses antidepressant augmentation. Her BMI is 22 and she has no medical problems. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Add lamotrigine 25mg daily with slow titration
distractors_rationale: 600mg is for mania, not depression.
CORRECT. After first-line quetiapine, lamotrigine is a NICE-recommended option for treatment-resistant bipolar depression. Slow titration required.
Aripiprazole is not effective for bipolar depression.
OFC is an option but lamotrigine is preferred after quetiapine.
Not indicated at this severity.
teaching_point: Bipolar depression treatment sequence (NICE): 1st: quetiapine or olanzapine. 2nd: add fluoxetine to olanzapine (OFC). 3rd: add lamotrigine. 4th: ECT.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder develops acute mania while on lithium (level 0.4 mmol/L). She is not pregnant. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Increase lithium to achieve level 0.6-1.0 mmol/L
Add olanzapine 10mg and check lithium level
distractors_rationale: Lithium alone is too slow for acute mania.
No need to switch.
CORRECT. Acute mania: add an antipsychotic (olanzapine) for rapid onset. Optimise lithium level (0.6-1.0). Check level: low at 0.4, may need dose increase.
Antipsychotic alone is fine, but lithium optimisation is also important.
Carbamazepine not first-line.
teaching_point: Breakthrough mania on lithium: add antipsychotic (rapid effect) AND optimise lithium level. Check adherence, check for drugs reducing lithium levels (NSAIDs, diuretics).

stem: A 48-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has had 4 manic episodes in the past 12 months despite good adherence to lithium (level 0.6 mmol/L). What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Add valproate and consider reducing lithium
distractors_rationale: Increasing lithium may help but adding another agent is more effective.
Carbamazepine is third-line.
CORRECT. Rapid cycling despite lithium: valproate has evidence for rapid cycling. BALANCE trial supports lithium+valproate. Lithium level 0.6 is therapeutic but mid-range.
LAI is an option but valproate augmentation has better evidence for rapid cycling.
Lamotrigine prevents depression, not mania.
teaching_point: Rapid cycling management: 1st: optimise lithium. 2nd: add valproate. 3rd: add antipsychotic. Rule out: hypothyroidism, substance misuse, antidepressant-induced cycling.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder on lithium develops coarse tremor, ataxia, and dysarthria. Lithium level is 2.3 mmol/L. She is on ibuprofen for arthritis. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Stop lithium, give IV normal saline, check U&Es, consider haemodialysis
Switch ibuprofen to paracetamol and continue lithium
distractors_rationale: Dose reduction alone is insufficient for level 2.3 with neurological symptoms.
CORRECT. Lithium toxicity (level >1.5 with neurological symptoms). Stop lithium, IV fluids, monitor U&Es. Haemodialysis if >2.5 or severe neuro symptoms. NSAID is the precipitant.
Propranolol treats benign lithium tremor, not toxicity.
Switching NSAID to paracetamol is correct but lithium cessation + active management is needed first.
Switching is for after recovery.
teaching_point: Lithium toxicity: level 1.5-2.5 moderate (vomiting, ataxia, dysarthria). >2.5 severe (seizures, coma). NSAIDs precipitate toxicity by reducing renal clearance. Paracetamol is safe.

stem: A 40-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium for 5 years. Routine bloods show TSH 12 mIU/L (0.3-4.2). He is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Stop lithium as it is causing hypothyroidism
Start levothyroxine 50mcg daily and continue lithium
distractors_rationale: Lithium can be continued with levothyroxine cover.
CORRECT. Lithium-induced hypothyroidism occurs in 10-20%. Management: start levothyroxine, continue lithium (mood stabilisation trumps thyroid effects). Monitor TFTs.
No need to switch if hypothyroidism is well-managed.
TSH 12 requires treatment, not monitoring.
Liothyronine (T3) is not first-line. Levothyroxine (T4) is standard.
teaching_point: Lithium and hypothyroidism: 10-20% develop subclinical/overt hypothyroidism. More common in women. Treatment: levothyroxine. Continue lithium. TFTs at baseline and every 6 months.

stem: A 38-year-old man with treatment-resistant depression (failed 2 antidepressants) is referred for assessment. On collateral, his partner reports he has 'high energy bursts' lasting 1-2 days where he is very productive and needs less sleep. These occur every few months. He has never been hospitalised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
distractors_rationale: Hypomanic episodes (even brief) suggest bipolar spectrum when TRD is present.
CORRECT. Bipolar II: hypomania (4+ days per DSM-5 but 2-3 days can still be bipolar II if clinically significant) + major depression. TRD with bipolar flags is highly suggestive.
Cyclothymia has subthreshold mood symptoms only.
Bipolar I requires mania (7+ days).
Too specific.
teaching_point: Brief hypomanic episodes (2-3 days) are common in bipolar II. DSM-5 requires 4 days but clinical judgement is important. Bipolar II is the most missed diagnosis in TRD.

stem: A 31-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder on lithium (level 0.7 mmol/L) and quetiapine 300mg nocte becomes pregnant. She is 8 weeks gestation. She has a history of severe mania requiring admission. What is the most appropriate management of her medication?
options: Stop quetiapine due to limited safety data
Continue both with close monitoring and adjustment
distractors_rationale: Lithium can be continued with monitoring.
Quetiapine is relatively safe in pregnancy.

CORRECT. Continue both medications with: (1) lowest effective doses; (2) monitor lithium levels 4-weekly; (3) detailed anomaly scan at 18-20 weeks; (4) monitor for gestational diabetes (quetiapine); (5) plan for neonatal adaptation syndrome. Risk of relapse if stopped: 50-90%.
Switching to lamotrigine mid-pregnancy risks destabilisation.
Switching mid-pregnancy is destabilising.
teaching_point: Bipolar in pregnancy: continue effective medication with monitoring. Lithium: Ebstein risk 1-2/1000. Quetiapine: relatively safe. Valproate: contraindicated. Relapse risk off medication: 50-90%. NICE CG192: individualised risk-benefit discussion.
